title: Open Codex and choose one practice folder
summary: Make an empty folder. Ask Codex to tell you exactly which folder it can see.
where: Use the ChatGPT desktop app on a Mac or Windows PC. Get it at chatgpt.com/download and sign in. An iPad can show these steps while you work on the computer. Some accounts also offer cloud or Remote tasks on iPad.

actions.title: Make a home for the test
actions.do: On Mac, click the blue Finder face and choose Documents. Choose File, then New Folder. On Windows, open Documents in File Explorer. Choose New, then Folder. Name it AI-Practice.
actions.see: AI-Practice appears in Documents. Open it and look inside.
actions.stuck: If that name is already in use, make AI-Practice-2. Use that name in each step.

actions.title: Find Codex
actions.do: Open ChatGPT on the computer. Look for the product menu and choose Codex.
actions.see: A task box and a list of projects appear. This is where you give Codex a job.
actions.stuck: If you see an ordinary chat, open the product menu again. These folder steps need the desktop app.

actions.title: Choose the folder
actions.do: Beside Projects, choose +, then Local and Next. Name the project Practice. Under Source folders, add your new folder. Choose Create project. If you see Open folder, use it to pick the same folder.
actions.see: Practice now points to the folder you made.
actions.stuck: If you picked all of Documents, go back. Choose the folder inside Documents that has your practice name.

actions.title: Check what it sees
actions.do: Start a chat inside Practice. Ask “Which folder is open? List its files. Leave them as they are.”
actions.see: Its answer should name your test folder. It has no files you made yet.
actions.stuck: If it lists your other documents, stop here and check the folder shown in the project.

roles: Open a folder of made-up mail rows.
Keep a small practice report together.
Give a new game its own home.

title: Make your first file with Codex
summary: Ask for two lines. Then open the actual file and check whether Codex wrote them.
where: On a Mac or PC, start ChatGPT, choose Codex and open your practice project. Use the folder from the first Codex lesson.

actions.title: Ask for two lines
actions.do: In the project’s chat type “Create status.txt in this folder. Line 1 is Queue checked. Line 2 is Ready to review.” Send the message.
actions.see: Codex should name the file it made.
actions.stuck: If the reply only shows the two lines, ask it to save them in status.txt in the open folder.

actions.title: Find the file
actions.do: Open that folder in Finder or File Explorer. Double-click status.txt. Read the two lines in the text editor.
actions.see: The first line reads Queue checked. The second reads Ready to review.
actions.stuck: If the file is missing, open the path in Codex’s answer and compare the folder names.

actions.title: Make a small edit
actions.do: Return to the same chat. Ask “Change just line 2 to Reviewed by owner. Keep line 1.”
actions.see: The task reports a change to status.txt.
actions.stuck: If it proposes a second file, repeat the name of the file you want changed.

actions.title: Read the saved result
actions.do: Close the file in the text editor and open it again from the folder. Compare both lines with your request.
actions.see: Queue checked stayed in place. Only the second line changed.
actions.stuck: If the old text is still visible, reload the editor and make sure the file lives in your practice folder.

roles: Update one line in a test mail checklist.
Keep a simple handoff note.
Edit a game title without losing its rules.

title: Read one changed line in Codex
summary: A before-and-after view helps you spot extra changes. Try it with the first line of a short file.
where: Use Codex in the desktop ChatGPT app. Open a practice Git repository, a project with saved checkpoints. It needs a saved README.md file. In GitHub Desktop you can choose File → New repository, name it ai-review-practice and select Initialize this repository with a README.

actions.title: Read the old heading
actions.do: Open README.md from the practice folder. Write its first heading on paper. A heading in this kind of file often starts with #.
actions.see: You have a copy of the old words to compare.
actions.stuck: If the file is blank, add a heading and save it as a Git checkpoint before the next step.

actions.title: Ask for an edit
actions.do: In Codex open this same folder. Type “Change only the first heading in README.md to # Practice Guide.”
actions.see: Codex lists an edit to README.md.
actions.stuck: If it lists more files, ask why they changed before doing anything else.

actions.title: Read the change view
actions.do: Open the task’s review pane and select README.md. If several turns appear, choose Last turn. Find the line marked minus and the one marked plus.
actions.see: The minus line is your old heading. The plus line is # Practice Guide.
actions.stuck: If both lines look alike, compare the words after #. A color change alone cannot tell you what was edited.

actions.title: Make a decision
actions.do: Read the lines around the heading. If an extra line was edited, name it and ask Codex to restore that line. Open the file again.
actions.see: You can point to the one planned change in the file.
actions.stuck: If the view has too much going on, compare the first heading with your paper copy first.

roles: Review a changed mail report heading.
Check edits to a shared note.
Review a game’s rule change.
sources: OpenAI · viewing changes and code reviews

title: Find the same Codex task on iPad
summary: Give one small job to a cloud computer. Open the job again on another screen.
where: Use chatgpt.com/codex on a computer or the Codex cloud area of the ChatGPT mobile app if your account has it. You need a connected practice repository. Cloud means the job runs on another computer.

actions.title: Open your cloud workspace
actions.do: Sign in to the account with access. On a computer, visit chatgpt.com/codex. On mobile, open Codex cloud tasks in the app if offered.
actions.see: The task list appears for the selected account.
actions.stuck: If you see someone else’s team name, switch to the workspace that owns your practice folder.

actions.title: Choose the source
actions.do: Open the environment picker. Choose your practice repository and look at its branch name. A branch is one copy of the work with its own changes.
actions.see: The chosen project name and branch match the files you plan to read.
actions.stuck: If your local Documents folder is missing, that is expected here. Choose a connected project.

actions.title: Give it a reading job
actions.do: Ask “Read README.md. Give me the first heading and the file path. Leave the files alone.” Start the task.
actions.see: The reply includes a heading and a path you can open.
actions.stuck: If the heading looks wrong, open the named branch and check its README.

actions.title: Find it on iPad
actions.do: Open the same workspace in the iPad app and find that task. Compare its heading with the file on GitHub.
actions.see: You can recognize the task by its request and the answer.
actions.stuck: If you see an empty list, check the sign-in and workspace first. Mobile access varies by account.

roles: Follow a mail report test away from the desk.
Reopen a task that reads a shared guide.
Check on a practice coding task from an iPad.

title: Make a four-line handoff with ChatGPT Work
summary: Turn four small facts into a note the next person can use.
where: Sign in at chatgpt.com or open the ChatGPT app on your computer or iPad. Work must be available on the account you choose.

actions.title: Choose Work
actions.do: In the desktop app pick ChatGPT from the product menu, then Work. On the web choose Work. On current mobile layouts, start a chat, tap the message box, then the model name and Work.
actions.see: A new Work conversation is ready.
actions.stuck: If Work is missing, check your account. You can still write the four-line handoff on paper.

actions.title: Give it the facts
actions.do: Type “Write a four-line handoff. Friday. Two test files checked. One file still open. The review desk owns it.”
actions.see: The draft keeps Friday, two checked, one open and the review desk.
actions.stuck: If it invents a deadline, ask it to point to the words that gave one.

actions.title: Fix one detail
actions.do: Reply “Change Friday to Thursday. Keep both counts and the same owner.”
actions.see: The day changes to Thursday. Two and one stay the same.
actions.stuck: If the owner changes too, name the line to restore and ask for another draft.

actions.title: Find the note later
actions.do: Return to Recents and reopen the Work conversation. Read the latest note. Check its day before you copy it.
actions.see: The latest handoff says Thursday.
actions.stuck: If Friday appears first, scroll to the later turn. The first draft can still be in the conversation.

roles: Hand off a sample mail check.
Summarize a review for the next shift.
Note which game tests still need work.

title: Give a ChatGPT project its own rule
summary: Keep related chats together and see whether a rule carries into a new one.
where: Open ChatGPT on the web, desktop or iPad. Sign in to the account where you want to keep the practice chats. Open its sidebar.

actions.title: Make the project
actions.do: Select New project, or choose the add button beside Projects. Name it Practice Handoffs and confirm.
actions.see: You see a new place with the project name.
actions.stuck: If the sidebar is hidden, open its menu before looking for Projects.

actions.title: Write a simple rule
actions.do: Open the project menu, then Project settings. Add “For a handoff use two headings: Decision and Next step.” Save the rule.
actions.see: The project settings show the two requested headings.
actions.stuck: If you entered the rule in a chat, copy it into the project instructions so a fresh chat can use it too.

actions.title: Try the rule
actions.do: Inside the project, start a chat. Choose Work if offered. Ask for a handoff from “Decision: keep the trial open. Next step: the test desk checks it Tuesday.”
actions.see: The reply gives the two headings and puts the facts under them.
actions.stuck: If the reply is free-form, make sure the chat sits inside Practice Handoffs.

actions.title: Start over in the same project
actions.do: Open another chat from inside the project. Say “The checklist is complete. The owner still needs to sign. Write a handoff.”
actions.see: The two headings return even though you did not repeat the rule.
actions.stuck: If they do not, reopen Project settings and check that the instruction was saved.

roles: Keep mail handoffs in one format.
Give a team’s trial notes two common headings.
Use the same test-note format for each game.

title: Add a tiny source file and check its numbers
summary: A project can reuse the same source in different chats. Start with two numbers you can add yourself.
where: Use a ChatGPT practice project. On Mac use TextEdit, on Windows use Notepad, or on iPad use a plain-text editor that saves to Files.

actions.title: Make counts.txt
actions.do: In TextEdit choose Format → Make Plain Text first. Type Ready 8 on one line and Waiting 3 on the next. Save as counts.txt. On iPad choose Save to Files from your editor.
actions.see: Opening counts.txt shows exactly two lines.
actions.stuck: If you see a rich-text ending such as .rtf, choose plain text and save the file again.

actions.title: Attach the file
actions.do: In the project open Sources. Choose Add source or the file upload control, then select counts.txt. On iPad use Browse to find its folder.
actions.see: The file name appears among the project’s sources.
actions.stuck: If you picked the wrong file, remove it from the practice project and attach the intended one.

actions.title: Ask about its numbers
actions.do: From a chat inside the project ask “Use counts.txt. How many are ready, how many are waiting and how many are there in all? Name the file.”
actions.see: The reply should say 8 ready, 3 waiting and 11 total.
actions.stuck: If it asks for the numbers again, check the source list and the name of the current project.

actions.title: Check the source
actions.do: Open your own copy of counts.txt. Add 8 and 3 yourself and compare your total with the reply.
actions.see: You can trace both counts to actual words in the file.
actions.stuck: If the reply gives only the total, ask for both lines that support it.

roles: Check a pretend mail queue count.
Verify a shared status total.
Keep level counts in one project file.

title: Open a dot and give it one small job
summary: A dot is a personal helper in ChatGPT. Give yours a room puzzle it can solve from three numbers.
where: Open ChatGPT in a desktop browser, in the desktop app or in the current iOS app on iPad. Dots needs supported access. Your plan, region and workspace can affect it. Mobile web does not support this exercise.

actions.title: Find Dots
actions.do: Sign in to ChatGPT. Choose Dots from the sidebar, or the Dot tab in the mobile app. Open your dot or pick the option to make one.
actions.see: Your existing dot opens, or the app walks you through setup.
actions.stuck: If Dots is missing, check that this account has access using the official guide in Sources.

actions.title: Give it a label
actions.do: Follow the setup steps. If asked for a name, use Practice Helper. Open its profile. For this puzzle, leave optional app and computer connections off.
actions.see: A conversation opens for your dot.
actions.stuck: If you already have one, use its existing conversation. You can skip making a new one.

actions.title: Ask the puzzle
actions.do: Type “Room A holds 8, B holds 12 and C holds 16. Which is the smallest room for a group of 11? Use only these numbers.”
actions.see: B fits 11. A is too small. C has spare seats you do not need.
actions.stuck: If it wants your calendar, explain that all three room sizes are already in the message.

actions.title: Change the group size
actions.do: Open the same dot conversation and say “Two more people are coming. What room do we need now?”
actions.see: The new total is 13. Only room C fits.
actions.stuck: If the answer uses a group of 2, remind it there were 11 people to start with.

roles: Choose a room for a pretend mail drill.
Check meeting space against a group size.
Plan a game table with enough seats.
sources: OpenAI · getting started with your dot

title: Check what a dot did after you asked
summary: Learn where to find a one-time task and how to correct the result.
where: Open the dot you already use in ChatGPT on desktop or iPad. Its profile on desktop gives you more space to see its activity.

actions.title: Ask for a one-time list
actions.do: Say “Make a packing list with one laptop, one charger and one adapter. Put the draft here and stop.”
actions.see: The dot posts three items in its conversation.
actions.stuck: If it offers to open files, say the three listed items are the whole source.

actions.title: Find its record
actions.do: Select the dot’s name or picture to open its profile. Look for the task or activity. Then return to this chat.
actions.see: You can match the list to the request you made.
actions.stuck: A quick answer might not have a separate task entry. The reply in the chat is still a record.

actions.title: Make a correction
actions.do: Say “The room has USB-C outlets. Drop the adapter and show my list again.” Count what remains.
actions.see: The new list has two items, the laptop and charger.
actions.stuck: If it keeps the adapter, point to the word drop and ask for the two remaining items.

actions.title: Check for a schedule
actions.do: Open Scheduled or look in the dot’s profile. Find where a repeating job would appear. This request was for one draft only.
actions.see: The packing task has no repeat time.
actions.stuck: If other schedules are already present, read their names to tell them apart. Leave their settings alone.

roles: Check a one-time mail report request.
Spot the difference between a draft and a repeating task.
Update one part of a game plan.
sources: OpenAI · getting started with your dot

title: Turn a packing list into a page
summary: A chat holds what you asked for. A page holds the list you want to keep and edit.
where: Use Space in ChatGPT on the web or desktop with an eligible adult account. Younger readers can use paper with an adult. Fold a sheet in half. Label one side Requests and the other Packing list.

actions.title: Collect three items
actions.do: In Work, type “Our ferry packing list is hat, water and notebook.” On paper, put these words on the Requests side.
actions.see: You have three starting items.
actions.stuck: If old items appear, start a fresh chat or a clean sheet.

actions.title: Make the page
actions.do: Ask “Make a page called Ferry Packing List. Put one item on each line.” Open it. On paper, write each item on the Packing list side.
actions.see: The page has a title and three lines.
actions.stuck: If your account has no Space entry, finish with the paper page.

actions.title: Edit one line
actions.do: Change water to water bottle. Leave hat and notebook in place. Read each line after the edit.
actions.see: There are still three items. Only the middle one changed.
actions.stuck: If it adds something new, ask for the original three items and the one change.

actions.title: Reopen the result
actions.do: In the sidebar open Space, then select the named page. On paper fold the Requests side away and read the actual list.
actions.see: Someone can pack from this page without reading your earlier request.
actions.stuck: If you opened the chat, follow the link to the named page inside it.

roles: Keep a mail test checklist ready to reuse.
Turn meeting decisions into a short page.
Keep the rules for a new game in one place.
